name: Neurofibromatosis Type 2

criteria.description: First-degree relative with NF2 AND unilateral VS or any 2 of: meningioma, schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity
Unilateral VS AND any 2 of: meningioma, schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity
Multiple meningiomas AND unilateral VS or any 2 of: schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Meeting any one of the above criteria. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas alone are sufficient. Gene-based criteria using NF2 mutation are sufficient.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: NF2 was reclassified in 2022 as NF2-related schwannomatosis. Very different from NF1 despite similar name. ~50% de novo. Mosaicism common (~25-33% of de novo cases).

pathognomonic.notes: Hallmark of NF2; bilateral in >90% by age 30; present in virtually all patients eventually

common.notes: Usually first symptom; gradual onset, bilateral

occasional.notes: May be the earliest finding; often detected in childhood
From vestibular schwannoma compression or surgical complication

occasional.symptomName: Cutaneous schwannomas or plaque-like skin lesions

rare.symptomName: Visual loss from optic nerve meningioma

laboratory: Audiometry showing sensorineural hearing loss (often asymmetric initially)
imaging: MRI brain with gadolinium: bilateral enhancing vestibular schwannomas
MRI brain: meningiomas (convexity, skull base, or posterior fossa)
MRI whole spine: schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas
genetic: Mosaicism in ~25-33% of de novo cases (milder phenotype, unilateral VS initially)
Truncating mutations associated with more severe disease than missense mutations
other: Slit-lamp examination for posterior subcapsular cataracts
Ophthalmologic exam for epiretinal membranes and retinal hamartomas

distinguishingFeatures: No vestibular schwannomas (or unilateral only with no other NF2 criteria)
NF1 has cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not schwannomas

redFlags: Sudden hearing loss (tumor hemorrhage or rapid growth)
Signs of brainstem compression from large vestibular schwannomas
Spinal cord compression from spinal tumors
Rapid tumor growth suggesting malignant transformation
Young child with unilateral vestibular schwannoma (consider mosaic NF2)
references: Evans DG. Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2): a clinical and molecular review. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2009;4:16.
Evans DG, et al. A clinical study of type 2 neurofibromatosis. Q J Med. 1992;84(304):603-618.
Plotkin SR, et al. Updated diagnostic criteria and nomenclature for neurofibromatosis type 2 and schwannomatosis. Neurology. 2022;98(7):295-303.
Asthagiri AR, et al. Neurofibromatosis type 2. Lancet. 2009;373(9679):1974-1986.
